content.what_is_it: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated, non-contagious systemic skin disease. In psoriasis, faulty immune signals cause skin cells to grow abnormally fast—in just a few days rather than the normal 3 to 4 weeks. These excess skin cells accumulate rapidly on the skin's surface, forming raised, thick, scaly, and often itchy or painful plaques.
content.how_common: Common chronic condition affecting millions of children and adults of all races and genders worldwide.
content.chronic_or_acute: Chronic, lifelong condition characterized by unpredictable cycles of flare-ups and periods of remission (with the rare exception of some children with guttate psoriasis whose condition may fully clear).
content.immune_pathophysiology: White blood cells called T-cells mistakenly attack healthy skin cells, triggering an inflammatory cascade. This causes hyperproliferation of keratinocytes (rapid skin cell production) and dilated dermal blood vessels, resulting in thick plaques and silvery scaling.

text:
Condition: Psoriasis
Section: Overview

What Is It: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated, non-contagious systemic skin disease. In psoriasis, faulty immune signals cause skin cells to grow abnormally fast—in just a few days rather than the normal 3 to 4 weeks. These excess skin cells accumulate rapidly on the skin's surface, forming raised, thick, scaly, and often itchy or painful plaques.
How Common: Common chronic condition affecting millions of children and adults of all races and genders worldwide.
Chronic Or Acute: Chronic, lifelong condition characterized by unpredictable cycles of flare-ups and periods of remission (with the rare exception of some children with guttate psoriasis whose condition may fully clear).
Contagious: Not Contagious
Immune Pathophysiology: White blood cells called T-cells mistakenly attack healthy skin cells, triggering an inflammatory cascade. This causes hyperproliferation of keratinocytes (rapid skin cell production) and dilated dermal blood vessels, resulting in thick plaques and silvery scaling.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)
Page: (AAD)/Psoriasis: Overview
Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/psoriasis/what/overview

content.name: Dry, Cold Weather and Low Humidity
content.threshold_risk: Low ambient temperature (< 10°C / 50°F) and low relative humidity (< 40%)
content.mechanism: Cold dry outdoor air and indoor artificial heating deplete epidermal moisture, causing thick scaling, cracks, fissures, and increased itching.
content.prevention_and_action: Apply thick ointment or cream moisturizers multiple times daily, use an indoor humidifier, protect exposed skin with warm cotton/soft clothing.

text:

Id: trig_dry_cold_weather
Name: Dry, Cold Weather and Low Humidity
Type: environmental
Weather Variable: temperature_and_humidity
Threshold Risk: Low ambient temperature (< 10°C / 50°F) and low relative humidity (< 40%)
Mechanism: Cold dry outdoor air and indoor artificial heating deplete epidermal moisture, causing thick scaling, cracks, fissures, and increased itching.
Prevention And Action: Apply thick ointment or cream moisturizers multiple times daily, use an indoor humidifier, protect exposed skin with warm cotton/soft clothing.

content.name: Severe Sunburn and Excessive UV Exposure
content.threshold_risk: High UV Index (>= 6) without sun protection leading to thermal erythema/burn
content.mechanism: While moderate, controlled sun exposure can improve psoriasis plaques, severe sunburn injures the epidermis and triggers the Koebner phenomenon, causing extensive new plaques.
content.prevention_and_action: Protect non-affected skin with broad-spectrum fragrance-free sunscreen (SPF 30+), limit direct sun sessions to brief safe durations, avoid tanning beds.

content.name: Skin Injury and Physical Trauma (Koebner Phenomenon)
content.threshold_risk: Cuts, scrapes, bug bites, surgical incisions, shaving nicks, tattoos, body piercings, or aggressive scratching
content.mechanism: Mechanical epidermal trauma triggers localized inflammatory signaling that leads to new psoriasis plaques appearing at the exact site of injury 10 to 14 days later.
content.prevention_and_action: Avoid tattoos and piercings; apply moisturizer before shaving to minimize cuts; treat cuts and bug bites immediately; avoid scratching or picking at scales.

content.name: Certain Prescription Medications
content.threshold_risk: Lithium, Antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine), Beta-blockers, Rapid withdrawal of oral systemic corticosteroids (prednisone rebound), certain NSAIDs
content.mechanism: Direct modulation of intracellular cAMP or immune pathways causing plaque exacerbation 2 to 3 weeks after starting, or sudden severe rebound pustular/erythrodermic psoriasis upon stopping systemic steroids.
content.prevention_and_action: Never abruptly discontinue medications; inform all prescribing physicians of your psoriasis diagnosis; taper systemic corticosteroids gradually under medical supervision.

bathing_protocol: Take only one bath or shower per day.
Limit showers to 5 minutes and baths to 15 minutes or less.
Use warm water every time—NEVER hot water, as hot water strips natural skin oils and worsens irritation.
Use a gentle, moisture-rich soap or cleanser formulated for sensitive skin; avoid deodorant soaps and abrasive scrubs.
Wash your skin very gently using your hands only—skip loofahs, sponges, buff puffs, and washcloths which can cause micro-trauma and flare psoriasis (Koebner phenomenon).
Rinse off cleansers thoroughly but gently.
Dry your skin gently by blotting water with a soft towel, leaving skin slightly damp.
moisturizing_protocol: Apply a fragrance-free moisturizer to all skin within 5 minutes of stepping out of the shower or bath to seal in hydration.
Thick creams or ointments (like petroleum jelly) work best for locking in moisture; apply a generous layer before bedtime.
Reapply moisturizer whenever skin feels dry or tight throughout the day.
itch_relief_and_scratching_prevention: Apply cool, damp compresses to itchy plaques to reduce inflammation and calm the urge to scratch.
Never scratch, pick, or peel psoriasis scales, as picking causes bleeding and worsens plaque thickness (Koebner phenomenon).
Keep fingernails trimmed short and smooth to prevent inadvertent skin trauma.

text:
Condition: Psoriasis
Section: Skin Care and Self Care

Bathing Protocol:
  - Take only one bath or shower per day.
  - Limit showers to 5 minutes and baths to 15 minutes or less.
  - Use warm water every time—NEVER hot water, as hot water strips natural skin oils and worsens irritation.
  - Use a gentle, moisture-rich soap or cleanser formulated for sensitive skin; avoid deodorant soaps and abrasive scrubs.
  - Wash your skin very gently using your hands only—skip loofahs, sponges, buff puffs, and washcloths which can cause micro-trauma and flare psoriasis (Koebner phenomenon).
  - Rinse off cleansers thoroughly but gently.
  - Dry your skin gently by blotting water with a soft towel, leaving skin slightly damp.
Moisturizing Protocol:
  - Apply a fragrance-free moisturizer to all skin within 5 minutes of stepping out of the shower or bath to seal in hydration.
  - Thick creams or ointments (like petroleum jelly) work best for locking in moisture; apply a generous layer before bedtime.
  - Reapply moisturizer whenever skin feels dry or tight throughout the day.
Itch Relief And Scratching Prevention:
  - Apply cool, damp compresses to itchy plaques to reduce inflammation and calm the urge to scratch.
  - Never scratch, pick, or peel psoriasis scales, as picking causes bleeding and worsens plaque thickness (Koebner phenomenon).
  - Keep fingernails trimmed short and smooth to prevent inadvertent skin trauma.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)
Page: (AAD)/Psoriasis: Baths and showers
Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/psoriasis/skin-care/baths-showers

text:
Condition: Psoriasis
Section: Flare-Up Management

Early Signs Of Flare:
  - Increased scaling and thickening of existing plaques
  - Appearance of new red or violet spots on skin
  - Sudden worsening of localized itch, burning, or soreness
  - Joint stiffness or swelling in fingers, toes, or lower back
Immediate Action Plan:
  - Resume or adjust prescribed topical treatments (e.g., topical corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues) as directed in your dermatologist's action plan.
  - Intensify emollient application using thick ointments.
  - Identify and manage recent triggers (stress, illness/infection, cold dry air, medication changes).
  - Contact your board-certified dermatologist if the flare spreads rapidly or is accompanied by systemic symptoms.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)
Page: (AAD)/Psoriasis triggers: Flare-ups due to triggers
Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/psoriasis/triggers/flares

content.description: Sudden widespread eruption of sheets of sterile pus-filled blisters covering large areas of the body, accompanied by high fever, severe shivering, intense burning pain, tachycardia, and profound fatigue.
content.urgency: Medical Emergency (Requires immediate emergency department admission)
content.action: Life-threatening condition requiring urgent inpatient medical stabilization, fluid/electrolyte management, and specialized systemic therapy.

Section: Red Flags and Warning Signs
Subsection: Warning Sign

Sign: Generalized Pustular Psoriasis (von Zumbusch)
Description: Sudden widespread eruption of sheets of sterile pus-filled blisters covering large areas of the body, accompanied by high fever, severe shivering, intense burning pain, tachycardia, and profound fatigue.
Urgency: Medical Emergency (Requires immediate emergency department admission)
Action: Life-threatening condition requiring urgent inpatient medical stabilization, fluid/electrolyte management, and specialized systemic therapy.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)

content.description: Widespread intense, fiery erythema and severe scaling covering >90% of the body surface area, accompanied by uncontrollable shivering, hypothermia, rapid heart rate, and swelling of the ankles/legs.
content.urgency: Medical Emergency (Requires immediate emergency department admission)
content.action: Life-threatening complication requiring immediate hospitalization due to high risk of hypothermia, severe fluid/protein loss, high-output heart failure, and sepsis.

text:

Sign: Erythrodermic Psoriasis
Description: Widespread intense, fiery erythema and severe scaling covering >90% of the body surface area, accompanied by uncontrollable shivering, hypothermia, rapid heart rate, and swelling of the ankles/legs.
Urgency: Medical Emergency (Requires immediate emergency department admission)
Action: Life-threatening complication requiring immediate hospitalization due to high risk of hypothermia, severe fluid/protein loss, high-output heart failure, and sepsis.

content.description: Swollen 'sausage-like' fingers or toes (dactylitis), persistent morning joint stiffness lasting >30-60 minutes, tender swollen joints, or heel pain (Achilles tendonitis / enthesitis).
content.action: Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent irreversible permanent joint destruction and long-term disability.

text:
Condition: Psoriasis
Section: Red Flags and Warning Signs
Subsection: Warning Sign

Sign: Early Signs of Psoriatic Arthritis
Description: Swollen 'sausage-like' fingers or toes (dactylitis), persistent morning joint stiffness lasting >30-60 minutes, tender swollen joints, or heel pain (Achilles tendonitis / enthesitis).
Urgency: Urgent Dermatologist / Rheumatologist Evaluation
Action: Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent irreversible permanent joint destruction and long-term disability.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)

Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/psoriasis/what/symptoms

content.relationship: Approximately 30% of patients with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis, causing joint inflammation, stiffness, dactylitis (sausage digits), enthesitis (heel pain), and potential permanent joint damage.

text:
Condition: Psoriasis
Section: Related Conditions
Subsection: Related Condition

Condition: Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA)
Relationship: Approximately 30% of patients with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis, causing joint inflammation, stiffness, dactylitis (sausage digits), enthesitis (heel pain), and potential permanent joint damage.
Type: Musculoskeletal Comorbidity

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)

Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/psoriasis/insider/other-conditions

content.relationship: Chronic systemic inflammation in psoriasis increases the risk of hypertension, atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction (heart attack), stroke, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).

text:

Condition: Cardiovascular Disease and Metabolic Syndrome

Type: Cardiovascular & Metabolic Comorbidity

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)

content.details: Supervised exposure to specific wavelengths of ultraviolet light (Narrowband UVB, Broadband UVB, PUVA - psoralen plus UVA, or Excimer laser) 2 to 3 times weekly. Slows rapid cell proliferation and dampens immune overactivity. (Note: AAD strongly warns against commercial tanning beds due to skin cancer risks).

content.indication: FDA-approved oral tablet for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and active psoriatic arthritis; does not require routine laboratory blood monitoring.

text:
Condition: Psoriasis
Section: Medications and Treatments
Subsection: Systemic Therapy / Oral / Biologic

Category: Oral Targeted PDE4 Inhibitor
Drug Name: Apremilast
Brand Name: Otezla
Mechanism: Oral phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor
Indication: FDA-approved oral tablet for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and active psoriatic arthritis; does not require routine laboratory blood monitoring.
Administration: Oral tablet twice daily.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)

Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/psoriasis/treatment/medications

content.details: Oral medications used for extensive, disabling psoriasis. Methotrexate suppresses immune activation (alcohol strictly avoided); Cyclosporine provides rapid clearance for severe flares (short-term use due to kidney/blood pressure risks); Acitretin is an oral retinoid (strict pregnancy contraindication).
content.administration: Oral medication under regular laboratory monitoring.

text:
Condition: Psoriasis
Section: Medications and Treatments
Subsection: Systemic Therapy / Oral / Biologic

Category: Conventional Systemic Immunosuppressants
Drug Name: Methotrexate, Cyclosporine, Acitretin
Details: Oral medications used for extensive, disabling psoriasis. Methotrexate suppresses immune activation (alcohol strictly avoided); Cyclosporine provides rapid clearance for severe flares (short-term use due to kidney/blood pressure risks); Acitretin is an oral retinoid (strict pregnancy contraindication).
Administration: Oral medication under regular laboratory monitoring.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)

Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/psoriasis/treatment/medications

content.details: Targeted biologic monoclonal antibodies that specifically block key inflammatory proteins (cytokines) driving psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. Highly effective for moderate-to-severe disease.
classes: TNF-alpha inhibitors (e.g., Adalimumab / Humira, Etanercept / Enbrel, Infliximab / Remicade)
IL-17 inhibitors (e.g., Secukinumab / Cosentyx, Ixekizumab / Taltz, Brodalumab / Siliq)
IL-23 inhibitors (e.g., Guselkumab / Tremfya, Risankizumab / Skyrizi, Tildrakizumab / Ilumya)
content.administration: Subcutaneous injection or intravenous infusion under regular medical monitoring.

text:
Condition: Psoriasis
Section: Medications and Treatments
Subsection: Systemic Therapy / Oral / Biologic

Category: Biologics and Biosimilars
Details: Targeted biologic monoclonal antibodies that specifically block key inflammatory proteins (cytokines) driving psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. Highly effective for moderate-to-severe disease.
Classes:
  - TNF-alpha inhibitors (e.g., Adalimumab / Humira, Etanercept / Enbrel, Infliximab / Remicade)
  - IL-17 inhibitors (e.g., Secukinumab / Cosentyx, Ixekizumab / Taltz, Brodalumab / Siliq)
  - IL-23 inhibitors (e.g., Guselkumab / Tremfya, Risankizumab / Skyrizi, Tildrakizumab / Ilumya)
  - IL-12/23 inhibitors (e.g., Ustekinumab / Stelara)
Administration: Subcutaneous injection or intravenous infusion under regular medical monitoring.

Source: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)
Page: (AAD)/Psoriasis: Diagnosis and treatment
Source URL: https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/psoriasis/treatment/medications
